extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants (Korean Intellectual Property Office / Korea)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting claim language and determining novelty/public availability (including product-by-function, limitation of use, product-by-process, Jepson claims, numerical/parameter limitations, and Article 30 grace-period exceptions) in patent examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of product-by-function/characteristic claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim specifies a product by its function, characteristic, etc., such an expression should, in principle, be construed as every product that has such function, characteristic, etc., except when it should be construed otherwise because the expression is specifically defined in the detailed description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner should not exclude the disclosed function/characteristic from the features of the invention when interpreting the claims. However, take into account common general technical knowledge at the time of filing — there are cases where a product described by function should not be construed as every product with that function (Example: 'means to selectively join plastic materials' should not apply to materials like magnetics which are difficult to join with plastic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of limitation of use (product specified by its use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim specifies a product by its use (limitation of use), the claimed invention should be interpreted only as a product specially suitable for the use disclosed in the claim, taking into account the specification, drawings, and common general technical knowledge at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a product includes all technical characteristics described in the claims, do not regard it as the claimed product when it is not appropriate for the relevant use or needs conversion to be used (Example: 'crane hook with a shape of ~' should be construed differently from 'fishing hooks' with regard to structure). If a product with a limitation of use is not suitable for that use per specification/drawings/common knowledge, the limitation of use has no impact in specifying the claimed invention and does not affect novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A product claim that defines a product by its manufacturing process should, in principle, be construed as defining the product per se; examiners should compare the claimed product itself with prior art when determining novelty and inventive step, unless there is a special reason in the claim description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special reasons to treat the product different from product-per-se should be accepted only in extremely exceptional cases (e.g., when it is greatly difficult to define the product in the ordinary way in the relevant technical field). If an identical product can be obtained by a different process, the claimed invention is not novel even if the applicant intended to limit the product to a specific process (e.g., 'Z obtained solely by process A' is still treated as the product per se). Example: a panel formed by a cutting process — if same panel exists, novelty lost despite process language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Jepson-type claims (preamble and body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even for Jepson-type claims dividing preamble and body, the invention should be specified as a whole including the preamble because claim type does not change technical scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not consider subject matter in the preamble publicly known merely because it appears there; whether preamble matters were publicly known is a factual question. The technical idea of the whole invention (including preamble) is the subject matter for patentability. The preamble can be construed as limiting field of invention, limiting applied product, or excluding scope of right — the body combined with preamble defines technical characteristics subject to protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly known invention' for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'publicly known invention' means an invention the contents of which have been known to an unspecified person without obligation of secrecy in Korea or a foreign country before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding cited inventions is carried out based on publicly known matters; take into account common general knowledge at filing — if a person skilled in the art can easily arrive at the matters described, those matters are considered publicly known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of common general technical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Common general knowledge means technologies generally known to a person skilled in the art (e.g., well-known art or commonly used art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Well-known art' includes technologies widely known in the relevant field (appearing in many prior art documents, widely known throughout industry, or well-known enough that examples are needless). 'Commonly used art' means well-known art used widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly worked invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'publicly worked invention' means an invention which has been worked under conditions where the contents of the invention are to be publicly known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient to decide whether the invention was publicly worked without deciding public knowledge. Public working can be established on the basis of matters embodied in machinery or systems; matters directly derivable from the facts considering common general knowledge as of the working can form the basis for finding a publicly worked invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'invention described in a distributed publication'
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention described in a distributed publication means an invention which is or potentially be described in a publication; 'potentially described' means a person skilled in the art can easily recognize the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an invention can be considered as an invention described in a distributed publication for novelty purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General considerations on what constitutes publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts kept secret by journals before release are not publicly known until contents are released; a company catalogue is considered a publication when produced unless special circumstances; if filing date equals publication date, novelty is retained unless filing time is clearly after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time of thesis publication is when the thesis is distributed to unspecified persons in public/university libraries after final examination, except when thesis contents were announced in public before final examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of determining novelty (compare claim vs cited invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine novelty by comparing matters defining the claimed invention and matters disclosed in the cited invention and extracting differences; if no difference exists the claimed invention is not novel; if there is a difference it is novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Substantially identical' means no newly produced effect because the difference is caused by mere addition/conversion/deletion of well-known or commonly used art and does not practically affect the technical idea of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty rules for inventions with numerical limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims with numerical limitations, a claimed invention is regarded novel when it is not identical to the cited invention even when numerical limitation not considered; specific rules apply when comparing numerical ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) If cited art lacks numerical limitation and the claim adds a new numerical limitation, the claim is regarded novel, unless the numerical value can be chosen by a person skilled in the art or is hinted by cited invention/common knowledge. (2) If claimed range is included in a cited range, novelty can still be acknowledged only by establishing criticality of the claimed range — requires detailed description of technical meaning, embodiments or supplemental materials proving criticality, and objective experimental confirmation across the range. (3) If the claimed range includes the cited range, novelty can be denied at once. (4) If ranges differ, novelty is generally acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and examination of parameter inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A parameter invention creates a nonstandard parameter and uses it as an essential element; because parameters may not precisely define subject matter, determination of inventive step should follow after clarifying subject matter from description, drawings, and common knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is determined by interpreting the parameter as part of the claims, but novelty cannot be confirmed solely because the parameter is novel. Novelty is generally denied if the parameter merely experimentally identifies nature/characteristics of a publicly known product or is merely an expression change. If reasonable doubt exists about identity with cited invention, examiner may await applicant's written arguments or experimental certificates after notifying reason for refusal; examiner must concretely describe ground of reasonable doubt and may propose ways to overcome it. These rules do not apply if parameter is standard, commonly used, or easily understandable to a person skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic vs specific concept comparison for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim and cited invention use generic or specific concepts, consider: (①) if claim is generic and cited is specific, the claim is not novel; (②) if claim is specific and cited generic, the claim has novelty unless the specific can be directly derived from the generic given common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'metal' claimed vs 'Cu' cited => claimed invention not novel. Conversely, a specific material (silver) in a specific use may be non-novel if using that material in that use belongs to common general knowledge and can be conceived without undue difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix novelty with inventive step (no combining multiple cited inventions for novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty determination shall not be conducted by comparing a claimed invention with a combination of two or more cited inventions; combination of references relates to inventive step, not novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: when a cited invention itself cites a distinct publication providing required detail, that distinct publication can be regarded as a cited invention. When a dictionary and a reference are needed to interpret a term in a cited reference, both can be cited as supporting references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Markush-type / multiple-embodiment claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims reciting multiple alternatives (Markush type), refusal may be notified on the ground that novelty and inventive step are lacking for each alternative invention with respect to a single prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a cited document contains more than two embodiments, do not determine novelty by combining two embodiments — combining embodiments concerns inventive step. Exceptional cases exist when one cited invention is obviously drawn from multiple embodiments in view of common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of applicant-admitted background technology
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant admits background technology in the specification or written opinion, an examiner may determine novelty by citing that background technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted background may be used as prior art for novelty determination claim-by-claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 30 (grace-period) exception — general rule and filing timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 30, an invention laid open by a person with the right to apply or publicly known against the applicant's intention may be considered not publicly known for novelty purposes if conditions are met and the application is filed within 12 months (6 months before March 15, 2012) of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant intending to take advantage must submit a written statement of intention when filing and documents proving relevant facts within 30 days of filing. The purpose is to encourage early publication and to allow applicants limited protection after their own disclosures. The exception does not apply to laid-open applications or published registrations under law/treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements when inventor laid open the invention before filing (Article 30(1)(1) case)
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim Article 30 protection where the inventor laid open the invention, the following must be met: (a) the invention was publicly known by the person with right to apply; (b) the application is filed within 12 months (6 months prior regime) of that public disclosure date (if disclosure date unspecified, use first day of month/year); (c) state purpose in the application; (d) submit documents proving relevant facts within 30 days of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also, the inventions must meet either subparagraph of Article 29(1) together with (a)-(d). For international applications, intention and documents must be filed within the domestic critical date per Article 201(4). Prove the discloser is the right-holder or successor; submit succession documents if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements when invention publicly known against applicant's intention (Article 30(1)(2) case)
rubrics_metrics.description: When disclosure occurred against the intention of the person with right to apply, the applicant must file within 12 months (6 months prior regime) of disclosure date to take advantage of Article 30, but does not need to state the purport of the exception in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof that the invention was disclosed against the applicant's intention must be supplied; the fact and required evidence are judged case-by-case and may be proved in various ways due to difficulty of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between disclosure by right-holder vs disclosure against intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Different evidentiary and procedural requirements apply depending on whether the invention was disclosed by the person with right to file or disclosed against their intention; common requirements include filing within the grace period and case-by-case examination claim-by-claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure was by a non-successor (someone not entitled), Article 30 may not apply. Determination depends on clear intention to lay open at the time of disclosure. Types of disclosure and required documents differ between the two cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and formality examination for Article 30 claims
rubrics_metrics.description: KIPO will conduct a formality examination to verify filing within the grace period and whether the invention was publicly known by a person with right to apply; identity of discloser and timing are checked; substantial examination assesses identity of publicly known invention and claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For exhibition disclosures, applicant may be invited to submit complementary documents to identify the invention shown (organizer, title, date, venue). If formality defects exist (discloser different from applicant/inventor, late filing beyond period, wrong disclosure date/type, insufficient evidence), the Office will notify to correct defects; failure to amend within period may invalidate the claim.
